title: Highly Suggestive of Financial Crime: 2,400 Mirror Trades, USD 6 Billion, and a Penalty for Systems and Controls

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The disgorgement figure is the Authority's own estimate of what the bank made from the failure: of a £163,076,224 penalty, £9,076,224 is "disgorgement" and £154,000,000 is "a penal element". The fee income is less than six percent of the fine.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise is in the breaches charged, and they are not the ones the headline suggests: Principle 3 (management and control) and SYSC rules 6.1.1 R and 6.3.1 R, over four years from 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2015. The Authority found "the AML control framework was substantially inadequate" in the UK arm of the Corporate Banking & Securities division — a finding about the absence of a control, not about the commission of an offence.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The mechanism was the fog. "There were more than 2,400 mirror trades between April 2012 and October 2014": a Russian customer of DB Moscow bought highly liquid Russian securities from DB Moscow for roubles, while "at the same time" a non-Russian customer of Deutsche Bank sold "the same number of the same securities" to Deutsche Bank in London. Each leg is an ordinary securities transaction. Only the pair is a transfer, and the pairing was arranged inside one office: "The orders for both sides of the mirror trades were received by DB Moscow's front office CB&S business (Moscow Front Office), which executed both sides at the same time." The non-Russian counterparty's onboarding "had been initiated and facilitated by Moscow Front Office" — the same desk introduced both halves of its own mirror.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is not the bank's and the Authority does not say whose it was. What the trades achieved is stated as a movement: they "were used by customers of Deutsche Bank and DB Moscow that were connected to each other to transfer more than USD6 billion from Russia, through Deutsche Bank in the UK, to overseas bank accounts, including in Cyprus, Estonia, and Latvia." No beneficiary is identified anywhere in the notice.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The resolution is the stage, and its shape is explicit. The bank self-reported — it "notified the Authority in early 2015 of concerns regarding its AML control framework after it commenced an investigation into a form of suspicious securities trading" — settled early, and took a 30 percent discount, reducing £229,076,224 to £163,076,224. The Authority goes as far as "The way these trades were conducted in combination with their scale and volume are highly suggestive of financial crime", notes that the matters "may give rise to additional investigation by other regulators and/or law enforcement agencies", and extracts an undertaking to cooperate with any such investigation. Suggestive, may, and an undertaking: a regulatory settlement that expressly leaves the criminal question to someone else.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A cross-border group structure in which a Moscow front office could book trades to London trading books, and a UK AML regime built on firms' own systems and controls — Principle 3 and SYSC — rather than on transaction-level official scrutiny.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A documented regulatory template for the mirror trade: a named pattern, a quantified flow, and a penalty calibrated almost entirely to deterrence rather than to profit, with a cooperation undertaking attached for the benefit of other agencies.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: A bank's own investigation produces the self-report; the self-report produces the early settlement and its discount; the settlement resolves the control failure and preserves the open question of what the flow was for. The conduct is established and its purpose is not, and the notice is what closes the matter.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the FCA's mirror-trading case documents a Russian laundering pipeline feeding Deutsche Bank's distressed real estate lending to a named American borrower — that the money and the mortgages are two ends of one proven chain.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: NOT ONE WORD OF THE SECOND HALF IS IN THE DOCUMENT, and this was checked by searching the full 44-page text: the Final Notice contains no occurrence of "Trump", none of "real estate", and nothing about property lending of any kind. It also names nobody at all — no customer, no beneficial owner, no counterparty. The Russian and non-Russian parties appear only as "a Russian customer" and "a non-Russian customer". There is no finding that any specific person benefited and no identification of where the USD 6 billion went beyond Cyprus, Estonia and Latvia. The node's original title asserted the connection; the title has been replaced, because nothing read supports it. The second thing to get right is what the Authority actually found. The breaches are management and control and systems and controls failures. On the trades themselves the furthest the Authority goes is that they "are highly suggestive of financial crime" — suggestive, in a notice that then hands the question on by recording that the matters "may give rise to additional investigation by other regulators and/or law enforcement agencies". No predicate offence is found. And the discovery was the bank's own: it notified the Authority in early 2015 after its own investigation, settled early and took a 30 percent discount. What remains, fully established, is still substantial: more than 2,400 paired trades over thirty months, USD 6 billion moved out of Russia through London, arranged on both sides by one Moscow desk that had also introduced the offshore counterparty.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: An FCA Final Notice to Deutsche Bank AG dated 30 January 2017 imposing a penalty of £163,076,224 — disgorgement of £9,076,224 and a penal element of £154,000,000 — for breaches of Principle 3 and SYSC 6.1.1 R and 6.3.1 R between 1 January 2012 and 31 December 2015, discounted 30 percent from £229,076,224 for early settlement. It finds the AML control framework of the UK Corporate Banking & Securities division substantially inadequate; records more than 2,400 mirror trades between April 2012 and October 2014 in which a Russian customer of DB Moscow bought highly liquid Russian securities for roubles while a non-Russian customer of Deutsche Bank simultaneously sold the same number of the same securities in London, both orders received and executed by DB Moscow's front office, which had also initiated and facilitated the non-Russian customer's onboarding; records that the trades were used by connected customers to transfer more than USD 6 billion from Russia through the UK to accounts including in Cyprus, Estonia and Latvia; states that the way the trades were conducted together with their scale and volume are highly suggestive of financial crime; notes the matters may give rise to further regulatory or law-enforcement investigation and records the bank's undertaking to cooperate with any such investigation; and records that the bank itself notified the Authority in early 2015 following its own investigation into the trading.

citations.title: Financial Conduct Authority, Final Notice to Deutsche Bank AG (Firm Reference Number 150018), 30 January 2017
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from fca.org.uk (341 KB, 44 pages) and read as extracted text. THE ACTION: "the Authority hereby imposes on Deutsche Bank AG (Deutsche Bank) a financial penalty of £163,076,224, comprising disgorgement of £9,076,224 and a penal element of £154,000,000, for breaches of Principle 3 (management and control) and Senior Management Arrangements, Systems and Controls (SYSC) rules 6.1.1 R and 6.3.1 R between 1 January 2012 and 31 December 2015". The bank settled early and so "qualified for a 30% (stage 1) discount"; without it the penalty "would have imposed a financial penalty of £229,076,224". NOTE WHAT THE BREACHES ARE: management and control, and systems and controls. The Authority found "the AML control framework was substantially inadequate" — not that the bank committed money laundering. THE TRADES: "The mirror trades were used by customers of Deutsche Bank and DB Moscow that were connected to each other to transfer more than USD6 billion from Russia, through Deutsche Bank in the UK, to overseas bank accounts, including in Cyprus, Estonia, and Latvia. The orders for both sides of the mirror trades were received by DB Moscow's front office CB&S business (Moscow Front Office), which executed both sides at the same time." "There were more than 2,400 mirror trades between April 2012 and October 2014": a Russian customer of DB Moscow bought highly liquid Russian securities from DB Moscow paying in roubles, while at the same time a non-Russian customer of Deutsche Bank — whose onboarding "had been initiated and facilitated by Moscow Front Office" — sold the same number of the same securities to Deutsche Bank in London. HOW FAR THE AUTHORITY GOES, AND NO FURTHER: "The way these trades were conducted in combination with their scale and volume are highly suggestive of financial crime." Suggestive. The Authority adds that "these matters may give rise to additional investigation by other regulators and/or law enforcement agencies" and that Deutsche Bank has undertaken "to cooperate with any other regulator or law enforcement agency that is investigating or commences investigating any of the facts and matters stated in this Notice". WHO REPORTED IT: "Deutsche Bank notified the Authority in early 2015 of concerns regarding its AML control framework after it commenced an investigation into a form of suspicious securities trading, referred to in this Notice as 'mirror trading', involving DB Moscow." The bank found it and told the regulator. WHAT THE NOTICE DOES NOT CONTAIN, CHECKED BY SEARCH OF THE FULL TEXT: not one occurrence of "Trump", "real estate" or property lending of any kind. No customer, beneficial owner or counterparty is named anywhere; they appear only as "a Russian customer" and "a non-Russian customer". There is no finding that any specific person benefited, no identification of where the USD6 billion ended up beyond the three jurisdictions listed, and no finding of a predicate offence. Any claim connecting these trades to any named individual's borrowing is outside this document and is not asserted by this dossier.
